## About {#about}



I am an economist working on **monetary economics, banking and macro-finance**. My research uses search-theoretic models of money to study how information frictions shape the banking system, liquidity provision and the transmission of monetary policy. I received my PhD from Tor Vergata University of Rome in September 2026 under the supervision of Fabrizio Mattesini. 

**Fields:** Monetary Economics · Banking · Macroeconomics · Financial Regulation · Payments · Search Theory

## Research {#research}

### Job Market Paper

::: {.paper .jmp}
[**Traditional vs. Shadow Banking in a Monetary Economy**](files/JMP.pdf)

<details open>
<summary>Abstract</summary>

Why do some depositors fund traditional banks while others fund shadow banks? This paper develops a monetary model of banking to provide an information-based explanation for the coexistence of traditional and shadow banks. Depositors can either monitor banks ex ante, at a cost that differs across households, or rely on costly ex post verification. Shadow banks attract depositors who monitor, while traditional banks attract depositors who rely on verification. The key mechanism links money demand to monitoring incentives: monitoring depositors earn a higher deposit rate and hold more money, which affects aggregate liquidity and the size of the shadow banking system, which in turn affects the incentive to monitor. With heterogeneous monitoring costs, monitoring decisions are either strategic complements or substitutes depending on the nominal interest rate. The model predicts a non-monotone response of the shadow banking system to the nominal interest rate. Because households ignore their effect on aggregate liquidity and on verification costs, the shadow banking system is too large at low interest rates and too small at high interest rates.

</details>
:::

### Working Papers

::: paper
[**Interbank Trade, Liquidity Reallocation and Welfare in a Monetary Economy**](files/Inter.pdf)
<span class="meta">with Paolo Varraso · *Revise and resubmit, Macroeconomic Dynamics*</span>

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>

We study positive and normative implications of interbank trade in a monetary economy
in which banks require liquidity to finance investment opportunities and meet bilaterally
to offset liquidity imbalances after these opportunities are realized. When the
nominal interest rate is low, the economy features an abundant-liquidity equilibrium. In
this region, we show analytically that either full participation or a complete shutdown of
the interbank market maximizes welfare, depending on the bargaining power of banks with
investment opportunities. When the nominal interest rate is high, the economy instead
features a scarce-liquidity equilibrium. In this case, full participation is optimal when
bargaining power is low. However, there are parameterizations of the model in which,
when both bargaining power and the nominal interest rate are sufficiently high, welfare
is maximized by restricting, but not fully shutting down, participation in the interbank
market.

</details>
:::

::: paper
[**Multidimensional Stock Market Liquidity and Business Cycles**](files/Multi.pdf)
<span class="meta">with Willem F.C. Verschoor and Luca M. Rolla  </span>

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>
Recognizing the difficulty in measuring stock market liquidity and its multidimensional nature,
we comprehensively analyze the impact of multidimensional stock market liquidity on business
cycles. Using the cross-sectional information contained in 7 different liquidity measures and
applying a factor model approach, we find that stock market liquidity includes information on
the future of the US. However, this information can differ significantly per liquidity dimension.
We find evidence that the illiquidity ratio and the trading volume are better suited to capture
information about the macroeconomy. In addition, we show that US liquidity measured by
the illiquidity ratio and trading volume also contains information about the state of the U.K.,
Canadian, and Australian economy. Finally, we show that the commonality in liquidity cannot
fully explain the relationship between stock market liquidity and the real economy. Our findings
exemplify the importance of liquidity proxies in explaining the state of the macroeconomy.


</details>
:::
